title: The Unexpected Question
description: Liars prepare answers for the obvious questions. They rarely prepare for the odd, sideways question that a truth‑teller can answer easily from real memory.
shortDescription: Liars prepare answers for the obvious questions. They rarely prepare for the odd, sideways question that a truth‑teller can answer easily from real memory.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Liars prepare answers for the obvious questions. They rarely prepare for the odd, sideways question that a truth‑teller can answer easily from real memory.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: After the standard “Where were you?” ask: “What color were the curtains in the room?” or “Who spoke first when you walked in?”

In a business setting, after a polished pitch, ask: “What was the hardest moment for you personally in building this?” Liars stumble; truthful people often smile ruefully and give a messy but real answer.
Police use: “What was the weather like?” or “What was on the radio in the car?”

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Truthful: pauses to recall, offers sensory detail, may say “I’m not sure, let me think.”
Liar: long pause, generic answer (“Nice, I think”), contradicts earlier details, or looks caught off guard and irritated.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I didn’t really notice…” (when it’s something most would notice)

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: The answer is vague or too perfectly aligned with their story.
They become defensive about the “irrelevant” question.
They repeat their script instead of answering the new question.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Liars rehearse a narrative. Unexpected questions force them off‑script, increasing cognitive load and exposing script gaps. Truthful memories have peripheral details because the event was lived.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Ask a question that is tangential but would be noticed by anyone in the situation.
Don’t reveal which details matter. Just gather information.
Use the “How” and “What” open‑ended questions that demand recounting, not “Yes/No.”

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Making the unexpected question so bizarre that even a truth‑teller would be puzzled. Keep it grounded.
Treating a single failed answer as proof. Some people genuinely don’t notice their environment.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A job candidate claims she led a major project. The interviewer asks, “What was the most annoying thing about the project management software you used?” The candidate freezes, then says, “It was fine.” A truthful project lead would have launched into a specific rant. The lack of any irritation detail betrays the lie.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Prepared lies are like painted backdrops: beautiful from the front, but step sideways and you see the cardboard.
